headline: The Kreditanstalt moves under CS Holding
text: Early in 1989 the Kreditanstalt turned CS Holding into a publicly traded umbrella company over the bank, the investment bank CS First Boston, and other holdings such as the utility Elektrowatt. The reorganisation cost about $80 million. Holders of Kreditanstalt bearer shares are offered CS Holding shares in exchange.
imageCaption: The Kreditanstalt headquarters on the Paradeplatz, Zurich

headline: The last Soviet soldiers leave Afghanistan
text: On 15 February the last Soviet military column left Afghanistan, crossing the Friendship Bridge at Termez into Soviet Uzbekistan; its commander, General Boris Gromov, crossed last. The withdrawal, agreed in the Geneva Accords of April 1988, began in May, and half the troops were gone by August. In more than nine years of war thousands of Soviet soldiers and hundreds of thousands of Afghans have died, and some five million Afghans have fled abroad, most of them to Pakistan and Iran. The Afghan government of Najibullah fights on with Soviet aid.
imageCaption: Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan, 1989

headline: Schlumberger's profit doubles
text: Schlumberger's operating results for 1988 rose to 419 million dollars from 211 million, excluding one-off items. Operating income in oilfield services tripled as North American wireline returned to profit, though oil price weakness hurt activity in the second half. It raised its stake in the Norwegian seismic company GECO from 50 to 75 percent.
source: Schlumberger 1988 annual report, chairman's letter dated 7 February 1989, https://investorcenter.slb.com/static-files/20c0ec6e-3664-4591-9972-cfee50f8ace3 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: A Schlumberger wireline truck, which lowers measuring tools into oil wells

headline: The Exxon Valdez runs aground in Alaska
text: Just after midnight on 24 March the tanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, and spilled about 11 million gallons of crude oil. The oil is spreading along a remote and rich coastline. Clean-up costs and lawsuits will follow; how large they will be is unknown.
imageCaption: Sea birds killed by the oil of the Exxon Valdez, Alaska, 1989
imageCredit: Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Trustee Council

headline: Buffett reveals a 600 million dollar bet on Coca-Cola
text: Berkshire's annual letter, dated 28 February, shows that in 1988 it bought 14,172,500 shares of Coca-Cola for 592.5 million dollars, worth 632.4 million at year end, and the maximum allowed stake in Freddie Mac. Buffett says Berkshire intends to hold such stocks for a long time. Net worth rose 20% in 1988.
imageCaption: A Coca-Cola can of the 1980s

headline: Berkshire soars 27% after its annual meeting in Omaha
text: Berkshire Hathaway shares jumped 27% in April to 6,275 dollars, against a market up 5%, after shareholders gathered in Omaha on 24 April for the annual meeting, the first since the share joined the New York Stock Exchange. Chairman Warren Buffett runs the company like no other: he buys businesses and large blocks of shares of companies with, as he puts it, "outstanding economics and outstanding managements", and then keeps them. "Our favourite holding period is forever," he wrote to shareholders in February, and he claims no opinion at all about where the stock market will be in a year. The method has lifted Berkshire's book value from 19.46 dollars a share in 1965 to 2,974 dollars at the end of 1988, 23% a year compounded. His latest purchase is a 593 million dollar stake in Coca-Cola.
source: https://www.berkshirehathaway.com/letters/1988.html (read 2026-10-03); price changes from data/out/brk.json and data/reference/sp500.json
imageCaption: Shareholders fill an arena in Omaha for the annual meeting of Berkshire Hathaway (photograph from 2025)

headline: Nintendo's Game Boy goes on sale in Japan
text: Nintendo released the Game Boy, a hand-held game machine, in Japan on 21 April for 12,500 yen. It has a black-and-white screen and runs for up to 30 hours on four AA batteries. It is due in America in the summer.
imageCaption: The original Nintendo Game Boy
imageCredit: Transfrom JPEG version and remove white background. Original by Evan-Amos.

headline: Intel announces the 486
text: Intel announced the i486 processor on 10 April at the Comdex show. It is the first x86 chip with more than a million transistors and, Intel says, about twice as fast as the 386 at the same clock speed. Samples are due in the third quarter.
imageCaption: The silicon die of an Intel 486 processor in its package

headline: The Bank of Japan starts raising rates
text: On 30 May the Bank of Japan raised its discount rate from 2.5% to 3.25%, its first increase in years, as it grows worried about soaring share and land prices. The Nikkei index ended May at 34,267, a quarter higher than a year ago. Land in central Tokyo has become so dear that the grounds of the Imperial Palace, little more than one square kilometre, are estimated to be worth more than all the real estate in California.
imageCaption: The Bank of Japan headquarters, Tokyo

headline: Tiananmen: China's army crushes the protests
text: Soldiers cleared Tiananmen Square in Beijing on 3 and 4 June in bloody clashes, ending seven weeks of protests that began on 15 April; martial law had been declared on 20 May. The number of dead is not known. Western nations have begun to impose arms embargoes on China. Prices had risen by about 30% in Beijing between 1987 and 1988, which fed the anger.
imageCaption: A lone man stands in front of a column of tanks at the entrance to Tiananmen Square, Beijing, 5 June 1989
imageCredit: Photo by CNN via Getty Images

headline: Khomeini dies; Khamenei becomes Supreme Leader
text: Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, leader of the revolution, died on 3 June aged 86. On 4 June the Assembly of Experts chose President Ali Khamenei as the new Supreme Leader. Millions of mourners filled Tehran for the funeral; in the crush people died and the body fell from its coffin, and a second ceremony had to be held.
imageCaption: Mourners at the funeral of Ayatollah Khomeini, Tehran, 4 June 1989

headline: Speculation about Japanese buyers lifts the bank shares
text: Swiss shares rose strongly in June, carried by foreign investors buying blue chips and by a favourable currency situation; they held up even when interest rates firmed and New York fell late in the month. Bank shares jumped in the third week on speculation that Japanese investors wanted to buy into Swiss banks, then fell back at the end of the month on rumours that a Swiss bank was involved in insider dealing in Germany.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 July 1989, p. 39 ('Zürcher Börse vom 26. Juni zum 30. Juni: Gegen Zinserhöhungen resistente Aktienkurse'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1989-07-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Swiss Bank Corporation's office in Basel, about 1920

headline: Shares climb back above their pre-crash record
text: The S&P 500 rose 9% in July to 346.08, and on 26 July it closed above its August 1987 record of 336.77 for the first time since the crash. Interest rates have fallen since the spring, and the Dow closed above 2,600 on 21 July.
imageCaption: President George H. W. Bush at his desk in the Oval Office

headline: Berkshire invests 600 million dollars in Gillette
text: On 21 July Berkshire agreed to invest 600 million dollars in Gillette through securities paying 8.75% that can be turned into about 11% of Gillette's shares after two years. Buffett called Gillette 'exactly the sort of business in which we like to invest for the long term'. Analysts see it as protection against hostile bidders.
imageCaption: A Gillette safety razor and a packet of Gillette Blue blades

headline: Four-for-one split and a 22% higher dividend
text: Philip Morris's board approved a four-for-one stock split and raised the quarterly dividend 22%, to 1.375 dollars a share before the split. The shares closed at 163.50 dollars. The company earned 1.34 billion dollars in the first half, on revenue of 22.4 billion against 15.4 billion a year earlier, thanks to Kraft.
imageCaption: Philip Morris's headquarters at 120 Park Avenue, New York
imageCredit: Eden, Janine and Jim from New York City

headline: East Germans flee to the West through Hungary
text: East Germany does not let its people travel to the West: a wall and a guarded border keep them in. But Hungary, another communist country, began taking down its border fence with Austria on 2 May, and on 19 August several hundred East Germans on holiday there rushed through a gate opened for a picnic at the border. Since 10 September Hungary lets all East Germans cross into Austria freely. At home, people in Leipzig have gathered every Monday since 4 September to demand change, despite arrests and beatings.
imageCaption: Removal of Hungary's border fence with Austria, 2009

headline: Apple's first portable Macintosh
text: Apple released the Macintosh Portable on 20 September, its first battery-powered computer, at 5,799 dollars. The Mac line is selling well.
imageCaption: The Macintosh Portable

headline: Sony buys Columbia Pictures
text: On 28 September Sony obtained an option to buy Coca-Cola's 49% stake in Columbia Pictures Entertainment for 27 dollars a share, as part of a takeover of the whole studio. The next day it agreed to buy Guber-Peters Entertainment for 200 million dollars and hired producers Peter Guber and Jon Peters to run Columbia.
imageCaption: The Columbia Pictures sign at the studio lot, Culver City

headline: Mitsubishi Estate buys Rockefeller Center
text: Mitsubishi Estate, the property company of the Mitsubishi group, is buying control of the Rockefeller Group, owner of Rockefeller Center in New York. It comes a month after Sony agreed to buy Columbia Pictures. Americans are uneasy about Japanese money buying up their landmarks.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Group (read 2026-10-03; cites New York Times, 31 October 1989); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Center (read 2026-10-03); data/news/1989.json
imageCaption: Mitsubishi Estate's president (right) and a senior vice president of the Rockefeller Group at the Tokyo press conference announcing the purchase, 31 October 1989
imageCredit: Photo by The Asahi Shimbun via Getty Images

headline: Friday the 13th: a failed buyout knocks the Dow down 7 percent
text: On Friday 13 October the Dow fell 190.58 points or 6.9% and the S&P 500 6.1%, after financing for a 6.75 billion dollar buyout of UAL, the parent of United Airlines, fell apart. The indexes had closed at records only four days earlier. The failure raises doubts about the junk-bond market that pays for such deals.
imageCaption: An options trader reacts at the opening of the London Stock Exchange on the Monday after New York's Friday-the-13th fall, 16 October 1989
imageCredit: Photo by Johnny EGGITT / AFP via Getty Images

headline: Machinists strike as Boeing struggles to build enough planes
text: Boeing's machinists went on strike on 5 October, demanding higher pay and less mandatory overtime. Many have been working seven-day weeks and up to 200 hours of forced overtime every three months as Boeing tries to keep up with orders; airlines ordered 322 757s alone in 1988 and 1989.
imageCaption: A Boeing 747 under assembly in the Everett plant, Washington

headline: Valdez bill of 880 million, and Exxon still raises the dividend
text: Exxon's third-quarter profit fell 9.4 percent to 1.11 billion dollars. In the second quarter it set aside 880 million dollars for cleaning up the Alaska spill, which cut nine-month profit by about a third to 2.54 billion. Even so, Exxon raised its quarterly dividend by 5 cents to 60 cents a share.
imageCaption: Crews washing an oiled beach in Prince William Sound, Alaska, 1989

headline: The Berlin Wall opens
text: On the evening of 9 November an East German spokesman, Guenter Schabowski, announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border, effective immediately as he understood it; that night crowds pushed through the checkpoints in Berlin and the guards gave way. It follows a year of change in eastern Europe, with free elections in Poland in June and Hungary opening its border. On 17 November mass protests began in Czechoslovakia.
imageCaption: East and West Berliners on the Wall in front of the Brandenburg Gate, the night after it opened, 10 November 1989

headline: The 'Germany boom': Daimler soars after the Wall falls
text: Since the opening of the Berlin Wall in November, foreign investors have been buying German blue chips, seeing West German industry as the main winner of the new markets in the East. The DAX reached a new post-war high before Christmas. In November the government allowed Daimler-Benz to take over MBB from 1 January, making it Germany's largest technology and defence group; Daimler also raised 1.9 billion marks by issuing new shares at 460 marks.
source: Die Zeit, 'Mehr Optimismus bei Ausländern', 1 December 1989, https://www.zeit.de/1989/49/mehr-optimismus-bei-auslaendern (read 2026-10-03); Die Zeit, 'Schöne Bescherung', 29 December 1989, https://www.zeit.de/1990/01/schoene-bescherung (read 2026-10-03); Die Zeit, 'Daimler/MBB: Prinzip Hoffnung', 24 November 1989, https://www.zeit.de/1989/48/prinzip-hoffnung (read 2026-10-03); Daimler-Benz Annual Report 1989, 'Allocation of Earnings' (capital increase of November 1989), https://bib.kuleuven.be/files/ebib/jaarverslagen/Daimler-Benz_1989.pdf (read 2026-10-03); Mercedes-Benz Classic, Illustrated Chronicle 1989 ('Mercedes-Benz AG formed', 29 June 1989), https://mercedes-benz-publicarchive.com/marsClassic/en/instance/ko/1989.xhtml?oid=4912361 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Chancellor Helmut Kohl at the opening of the Brandenburg Gate border crossing, Berlin, 22 December 1989

headline: 1989 in review: up 27 percent and above the 1987 peak
text: The S&P 500 gained 27% in 1989 to 353.40, its best year since the bull market began, and the Dow rose 27.0% to 2,753.20. Both are now above their pre-crash records. The October scare raised doubts whether the takeover boom, which drove much of the rise, can keep finding borrowed money.
imageCaption: American shares (S&P 500) at the end of each month of 1989: up 27 percent in the year
imageCredit: Chart: Month by Month. Data: Yahoo Finance (^GSPC, month-end closes)

headline: Revolutions sweep the rest of eastern Europe
text: Presidents Bush and Gorbachev met off Malta on 2 and 3 December. In Prague the communists gave up power after weeks of peaceful protest, and the dissident playwright Vaclav Havel was elected president on 29 December. In Romania an uprising that began in Timisoara on 16 December reached Bucharest, and the dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was executed on 25 December.
imageCaption: Crowds face tanks and militia on Magheru Boulevard in Bucharest during the Romanian revolution, December 1989

headline: IBJ among the world's most valuable companies as Tokyo hits a record
text: The Nikkei 225 hit a record intraday high of 38,957 on 29 December, six times its level at the start of the decade, despite another rate rise to 4.25% on 25 December. By some counts the Industrial Bank of Japan is now the most valuable company in the world, worth more than 100 billion dollars, ahead of Exxon.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikkei_225 (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_asset_price_bubble (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Bank_of_Japan (read 2026-10-03); data/news/1989.json for the 104 billion dollar estimate (finance.yahoo.com source could not be re-fetched)
imageCaption: The trading hall of the Tokyo Stock Exchange

headline: IBM to cut 10,000 jobs
text: IBM said it will cut 10,000 US jobs through retirement and separation incentives, setting aside 2.3 billion dollars of pre-tax profit, and will buy back another 4 billion dollars of its own shares. It blames sluggish spending by American companies, and personal computers and workstations are now powerful enough to take work away from expensive mainframes. Sales growth has slowed to single digits.
imageCaption: IBM System/370, 1972
